name: MicroK8s
license: Apache 2.0 (bundled components keep their own licences, e.g. dqlite is LGPLv3 with a static-linking exception)
summary: Canonical’s Kubernetes in one snap package: installs with one command on Linux, forms a highly available cluster by itself at three nodes, and adds features as addons.
intro: MicroK8s is upstream Kubernetes packaged as a snap, the self-contained, auto-updating package format from Ubuntu. `snap install microk8s` puts the Kubernetes services, containerd and a bundled `microk8s kubectl` on any Linux distribution that runs snapd. There is no VM and no node container: the services run directly on the host as systemd units, and since version 1.21 the API server, scheduler, controller manager, kubelet and kube-proxy run as subprocesses of a single `kubelite` daemon. Cluster state lives in dqlite, Canonical’s Raft-replicated version of SQLite, behind a drop-in replacement for etcd, and pods are networked by Calico (with the `ha-cluster` addon turned off, MicroK8s falls back to etcd and Flannel). Each snap channel, such as `1.36/stable`, follows one Kubernetes minor version.

Canonical calls it “a low-ops, minimal production Kubernetes”, scalable “from a single node to a high-availability production cluster”. `microk8s add-node` prints a join command; once three or more nodes have joined, high availability switches on by itself, every node runs the control plane, and at least three of them vote on the replicated datastore. Everything beyond the core (DNS, storage, ingress, the GPU operator and dozens more) is an addon you `enable` or `disable`. The same snap is pitched at laptops, CI runners, Raspberry Pis and appliances; on macOS and Windows an installer runs it inside a Multipass Ubuntu VM. Unlike K3s, a single binary you copy onto any Linux host, MicroK8s depends on snapd, and it replicates state with dqlite rather than etcd. It is free, with paid support through Ubuntu Pro.
strengths: One command installs conformant Kubernetes on many Linux distributions, and a snap channel pins the minor version while patch updates arrive automatically
High availability forms by itself at three nodes, with no separate etcd cluster or load balancer to build
Addons switch on common pieces such as DNS, hostpath storage, ingress or the GPU operator with one command
Runs in as little as 540 MB of memory, and an optional strictly confined snap walls it off from the host with AppArmor, seccomp and namespaces
limits: Tied to snapd: native only on Linux with snaps; on macOS and Windows it runs in a Multipass VM that needs at least 4 GB of RAM and 40 GB of storage
Follows upstream with a lag: in October 2026 the newest channel is 1.36 (May), while Kubernetes 1.37 shipped in August
Its HA datastore is dqlite rather than the usual etcd; a lost quorum needs a manual recovery procedure, and electing a new leader after a crash takes up to 5 seconds
Strict confinement blocks workloads that need shared mounts with the host (the Cilium, GPU and Multus addons need the classic snap), and addons come and go: 1.36 removed the dashboard

story: Canonical launched MicroK8s on December 6, 2018 as “a fast and efficient upstream Kubernetes delivered as a single snap package that installs on 42 flavours of Linux”. It installed conformant Kubernetes 1.13, and its first add-ons included a container registry, storage and GPU enablement. The launch named its use cases: embedded, auto-updating Kubernetes for IoT, local CI/CD pipelines, disposable clusters inside production pipelines, single-node servers and machine-learning work with Kubeflow.

High availability arrived with MicroK8s 1.19 in August 2020: cluster at least three nodes and the datastore, dqlite, replicates itself with Raft, with no extra setup. Version 1.21 (April 2021) folded the separate Kubernetes services into one `kubelite` binary and brought major dqlite stability fixes.
Canonical now pitches the same package to developers, DevOps teams and software vendors who embed Kubernetes in appliances, and sells support for it through Ubuntu Pro.

choices.why: The launch post gave the reasons: automatic updates keep developers on the latest upstream release, and snaps have well-defined security capabilities. Channels let users stay on one minor version, and a strictly confined variant isolates it further.

choices.choice: dqlite instead of etcd for HA
choices.why: Canonical wanted HA with almost no operations. Every node runs the control plane, and nodes take database roles (voter, standby, spare) automatically, so an administrator only adds or removes nodes and never runs a separate etcd cluster.
Installing only core Kubernetes keeps the footprint small for small devices; DNS, storage, ingress, GPUs and the rest are switched on only where needed.

timeline.text: Launched on December 6 as a snap with Kubernetes 1.13
1.19 adds automatic high availability on dqlite (August)
1.21 runs the Kubernetes services in one kubelite binary (April)
1.36 in May drops the dashboard addon after its upstream deprecation
